correctness.rationale: Fix a nontrivial finite open cover \(\mathcal U=\{U_j\}\) of the inverse limit and an infinite time set. For each non-dense \(U_j\), choose an open hole \(O_j\subset X\setminus\overline{U_j}\). Finite-coordinate cylinder neighborhoods of finitely many chosen points in these holes can be pushed to one common stage \(r\), giving nonempty open \(V_j\subset X_r\) with \(\pi_r^{-1}(V_j)\subset O_j\). Choose closed \(F_j\subset V_j\) with nonempty interior and put \(W_j=X_r\setminus F_j\). Surjectivity of \(\pi_r\) proves that the \(W_j\) cover \(X_r\): otherwise a stage point in all \(F_j\) lifts to a point omitted by every \(U_j\). Thus \(\mathcal W=\{W_j\}\) is nontrivial and \(U_j\subset\pi_r^{-1}(W_j)\). Equivariance commutes with the joins, and surjectivity gives \(N(\pi_r^{-1}\mathcal C)=N(\mathcal C)\), so the inverse-limit cover complexity dominates the full-scattering stage complexity and diverges. The countable-product corollary then follows by taking the inverse sequence of finite products and using the published finite-product theorem.
residual_risks: The proof requires surjective bonding maps; no claim is made for arbitrary inverse systems.
The theorem is qualitative and inherits no uniform divergence rate beyond a chosen stage.
